intro: The landscape starts to dissolve, then lines and color begin to carry the composition themselves. Each example treats abstraction as a distinct sequence of choices.
alt: Four studies show an intensely colored mountain scene, floating geometry, open rhythmic marks and thick bands of spectral color.

variants.name: Der Blaue Reiter
variants.look: Hills remain barely recognizable as simplified outlines filled with non-naturalistic colors.
variants.history: Der Blaue Reiter was an informal group around Munich in the early 1910s. Its artists pursued different ways to explore expression, color and spirituality.
variants.when: Study the point where a color can suggest a feeling while a landscape remains recognizable.
variants.why: Simplification frees the relationships between shapes and colors to do more expressive work.

variants.name: Suprematism
variants.look: Slanted blocks float against a pale ground. Their size, direction and distance distinguish them.
variants.history: Kazimir Malevich presented Suprematism publicly in Russia in 1915. The movement made arrangements of geometric forms central to the image.
variants.when: Study a few elementary shapes when you want placement and pressure between them to become the subject.
variants.why: The limited set of ingredients makes a small shift in balance easy to see.

variants.name: early pure abstraction
variants.look: Open areas, loops and small weighted shapes occupy different parts of the same field.
variants.history: In the early twentieth century, artists in many settings developed nonrepresentational art in parallel. They reached it by distinct paths through music, geometric experiment, color and more.
variants.when: Study whether a few areas of line or color can organize a whole image without depending on recognizable objects.
variants.why: The eye builds relationships from timing, balance and repeated intervals.

variants.name: Synchromism
variants.look: Curving bands of intense color seem to turn like pieces of a volume.
variants.history: American artists Morgan Russell and Stanton Macdonald-Wright developed Synchromism in the 1910s, using color relationships to organize abstract compositions.
variants.when: Study it when you want color itself to make passages come forward or send them back.
variants.why: Sequences of related colors can suggest that a single mass bends, expands or turns.

prompt: Educational art style comparison board. Exactly four square panels arranged as a 2×2 grid in stated reading order, hairline neutral dividers. Recurring original character is an adult woman with ash-blonde hair in a neat low bun, four-color square hair clip, black rectangular glasses worn throughout, black blazer over knee-length black sheath dress, blue lanyard, blank badge, white coffee mug with four colored squares. As specified, she is the subject of each individual artwork's idiom, or a visitor for works that do not depict people. Style distinctions are immediately clear. Scene list in exact order: Der Blaue Reiter: modern woman within a still-recognizable mountain motif dissolved in electric non-natural color and energetic outlines; Suprematism: sparse study of diagonally tilted black red and ochre geometries floating on white, woman is observer by edge of canvas; early pure abstraction: balanced nonfigurative composition of rhythmic and weighted loops, tiny geometric forms and washy fields, woman as visible observer; Synchromism: curving stepped bands of spectral color like a spiral staircase with color-value tension, character again viewing from lower corner. No lettering, captions, watermark or ornamental frame.
